title: Logic Gates: AND, OR, NOT
objective: After this level you can explain how AND, OR and NOT gates turn yes-or-no inputs into a yes-or-no output.
summary: Logic gates turn yes-or-no inputs into one output: AND needs all 1s, OR any 1, NOT flips. Boole wrote the algebra; Shannon showed switches could do it.

cards.headline: A lamp with two switches can already do logic.
cards.body: Wire a lamp so it lights only when both of two switches are closed. That lamp is answering a question: is switch A on, and is switch B on? Computers are built from tiny deciders just like it.

cards.headline: AND, OR, NOT: three ways to decide

items.label: AND
points: Outputs 1 only if every input is 1
Like two switches in series: both must close

items.label: OR
points: Like two switches in parallel: either one will do

cards.headline: Gates are switches in disguise
cards.body: A logic gate takes yes-or-no inputs, 1s and 0s, and produces one yes-or-no output. It works like a switch, passing or blocking electrical pulses, and its circuits are built from parts such as transistors, the same on-off switches that store Level 2's bits. Wire gates together and they can even do arithmetic. That's the next level's trick.

cards.headline: The math came first
cards.body: In 1847 and 1854 George Boole worked out an algebra of logic, now called Boolean algebra, in which statements are simply true or false, written 1 or 0. Much later, Claude Shannon's master's thesis used Boolean algebra to lay the theoretical groundwork for digital circuits. In other words, circuits full of switches could be worked out with algebra, on paper.

cards.headline: Gates: decided
learned: AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1
OR outputs 1 if any input is 1; NOT flips its input
Gates act like switches and are built from transistors
Boole wrote the algebra; Shannon applied it to circuits

questions.prompt: An AND gate that gets the inputs 1 and 0 outputs _____.

options.rationale: That is what an OR gate would give.
A gate has a single one-bit output.

options.label: both 1 and 0
options.rationale: A gate gives exactly one output.

questions.explanation: AND outputs 1 only when every input is 1, so 1 and 0 give 0.

questions.prompt: Match each logic gate with what it does.

pairs.right: Outputs 1 only if every input is 1

questions.explanation: AND outputs 1 only if every input is 1, OR outputs 1 if any input is 1, and NOT flips its one input, which is why it's also called an inverter.

questions.prompt: Boole's algebra works with true and false. How does that fit a computer's bits?

options.label: True and false map to 1 and 0, a bit's two values
Boole invented the transistor to store them
options.rationale: Boole worked on logic in 1847 and 1854, long before transistors.

options.label: Each statement needs a full byte, with 256 values
options.rationale: True or false is a single two-way choice: one bit.

options.label: Bits can only store numbers, not logic
options.rationale: A 1 or 0 can stand for true or false.

questions.explanation: Boolean algebra writes true as 1 and false as 0: exactly one bit.
